verses.note: The first thing Scripture calls holy is a day. Holiness here means belonging to God in a special way, and time is claimed before any place or person is. Israel's sacred calendar, and later the Christian Lord's Day, grow from this root.

Joseph's reasons begin with loyalty to Potiphar but end with God. A sin against a neighbor is first a sin against God, which is how David will later confess his adultery (Psalm 51:4). Holiness here is not ritual separation but faithfulness in a private room with no one watching.

Holiness here is not a property of the soil but of God's presence, which makes an ordinary hillside a place to be approached with reverence and limits. The verse teaches that God's nearness and God's otherness come together: he calls Moses close and tells him how close he may come.

The people cannot stay close to the place where God speaks. Their distance is not simply fear but a right perception of the gulf between the holy God and sinful people, which the following verses address with a mediator.

Holiness here means keeping human craft and human exposure away from the place where God meets his people. The altar is to be something God gives rather than something humans display their skill in, and worship is to be free of the sexual display that marked some neighboring cults.
After the calf, the approach to God is narrowed to one mediator. The people's sin has made the distance greater than before, and even their animals are kept away from the holy mountain.

Even the high priest, on the appointed day, in the right clothing, cannot look on the place of God's presence. The incense cloud screens him from a sight that would kill him, as Moses was hidden in the rock when God's glory passed (Exodus 33:20-22).

The things that carried impurity away also pass impurity to those who handle them, so the men who serve in the rite must wash before returning. The same paradox appears with the ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19:7-10): what cleanses the community leaves those who administer it needing cleansing.
The law refuses a category of ordinary, neutral killing for these animals. Taking an animal's life for food is brought inside the sphere of worship, so that even the family meal is answerable to God.
Impurity is not the same as sin. Eating a carcass defiles, but washing and waiting until evening restore cleanness; only refusing the remedy turns impurity into guilt.
God's words mark both private and public space. The home and the town gate, where justice was done, are equally to be governed by what God has said.

Jerusalem is called ir haqqodesh, "the holy city", and the promise is that nothing unclean will enter it again. Revelation's new Jerusalem takes up the same promise: nothing unclean will ever enter it (Revelation 21:27). Holiness here is God's gift to the city, not an achievement it maintains.

Leaving Babylon is not only a change of address but a separation from its uncleanness. The New Testament applies the call to the church's separation from idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:17) and to God's people coming out of the Babylon of Revelation (Revelation 18:4).

Jerusalem is called righteous and holy not because of what it had been, since Jeremiah's whole book indicts it, but because of what God will make it. Holiness here is a gift of restoration, as the chapter's last verse will say of the whole city (verse 40).

Holiness spreads outward here, from the temple to the city to its unclean valley. In the law, contact with the unclean defiled the holy; in the promise, God's holiness overtakes the unclean. The vision of the new Jerusalem in Revelation, where nothing unclean enters and the whole city is God's dwelling (Revelation 21:22-27), develops the same hope.
The holiness God defends is not a remote purity but his standing as the true God before the watching nations. Israel's restoration is God's self-vindication.

Holiness in this verse is something God gives, not something Israel achieves. The same God who is profaned by his people's sin (36:20) is displayed as holy by his presence in a people he has cleansed.

The victory is pictured in the language of the altar. The people God defends become like the temple's holy vessels, a picture that anticipates Zechariah 14:20-21, where even ordinary cooking pots in Jerusalem become holy to the LORD.
The call to be perfect restates Leviticus's call to holiness in terms of love. God's perfection in this context is his indiscriminate generosity, and the disciple's perfection is to share it.
Holy things are to be treated as holy. The verse guards against casualness with what belongs to God, the same concern as the laws about sacrificial food.
The encounter is between the Holy One of God and an unclean spirit. Holiness is not fragile in Jesus: it does not retreat from uncleanness but drives it out.
Under the law, uncleanness spreads by touch. In Jesus, holiness spreads instead. The touch shows a purity that is contagious, reversing the old direction.
The temple was set apart for God, and Jesus treats its courts, even the outermost, as holy ground that may not be used for convenience or gain.
God's power and holiness are not set against his mercy; they are its source. The one whose name is holy stoops to those who fear him.
Nearness to Jesus' power makes Simon aware of the distance between himself and holiness. The fitting response to God's presence is not pride at being near it but confession.

Under the Law uncleanness spreads by contact. Here holiness spreads instead: Jesus' touch communicates cleanness, reversing the direction of contagion and showing a holiness that heals what it touches.
Leviticus says ‘Be holy, for I am holy’; Jesus says ‘Be merciful, as your Father is merciful’. In Luke, mercy is the shape holiness takes toward sinners and enemies.
Paul locates holiness in the body: hands, eyes, tongue, and every member are to be placed at God's disposal. Christian holiness is not a retreat from bodily life but its reassignment to a new master.
Election has a moral goal: to be holy and blameless before God. Paul gives no ground for the idea that being chosen makes holiness unnecessary; the choice aims at it.
The holiness the law demanded of the high priest and could only approximate is found fully in Jesus. His sinlessness (4:15) is not an abstraction but the qualification for his office.

Graded access (priests to the outer room, the high priest alone to the inner, once a year, with blood) taught Israel that God's holiness cannot be approached casually. The whole arrangement was a lesson in distance, which the next verse interprets.
